meta.title: Who really said "If you love something, set it free. If it comes back, it's yours; if it doesn't, it never was"? | Quotle.info
meta.description: No — Kahlil Gibran never wrote this. Quote Investigator traced it to an anonymous 1969–1972 saying with no known author. The Gibran credit is a myth.
meta.ogTitle: Who really said 'If you love something, set it free. If it comes back, it's yours; if it doesn't, it never was'?
meta.ogDescription: Not Kahlil Gibran. It's an anonymous modern maxim first documented 1969–1972 — the true author was never identified.

answer.label: Not Kahlil Gibran — an anonymous modern maxim
answer.sourceLine: This line is not found in any work by Kahlil Gibran. Quote Investigator ↗ traced it and concluded “the creator of this general saying is not known.” Its earliest full versions appear in educator Jess Lair’s 1969 book (submitted anonymously by a student) and a 1972 Peter Max comic panel that credited it to “Unknown.” It was later pinned on famous names — Gibran, Richard Bach, and others — with no supporting source.

source.excerpt: If you love something, set it free. If it comes back, it is yours. If it doesn’t, it never was.
trail: A 1969 version in Jess Lair’s I Ain’t Much, Baby—But I’m All I’ve Got reads “If you want something very, very badly, let it go free…” — submitted anonymously by a student, per Quote Investigator ↗.
A compact form matching today’s wording appeared in a 1972 Peter Max comic panel that credited it to “Unknown” ↗.
Quote Investigator’s conclusion is unambiguous: “the creator of this general saying is not known ↗.”

author.name: Kahlil Gibran
author.heading: Why Gibran gets the credit
author.metaLine: 1883–1931 · Lebanese-American poet, author of The Prophet
author.bio: Kahlil Gibran (1883–1931) was a Lebanese-American poet, painter and author, best known for The Prophet (1923), a book of poetic essays on love, marriage and freedom that has sold tens of millions of copies. Because Gibran wrote so movingly about loving without possessing, he became a natural magnet for feel-good sayings on the theme — and this anonymous maxim was retro-fitted onto his name. The line does not appear in The Prophet or his other works.

misattribution.heading: A magnet-name misattribution
misattribution.intro: This warm, symmetrical maxim is one of the internet’s most-passed-around lines, and it has been pinned on several famous names — none of whom can be shown to have written it.

items.why: The line does not appear in The Prophet or any Gibran text, yet a near-identical “let them go” version still circulates under his name (see BrainyQuote ↗). Quote Investigator ↗ traces the saying to anonymous 1969–1972 sources and attributes it to no named author.
By the 1990s the line was widely assigned to novelist Richard Bach, but QI “found no substantiation that Richard Bach created” it, and it is not in his novels — per Quote Investigator ↗.
Lair printed a 1969 version in I Ain’t Much, Baby—But I’m All I’ve Got, but it was submitted to him anonymously by a student — he never claimed authorship, per Quote Investigator ↗.

misattribution.truthLine: The honest answer: the author is unknown. The saying is anonymous folk wisdom first documented around 1969–1972 — “the creator of this general saying is not known” ↗.

context.heading: Why it spread
lead: The line owes its virality to its neat, self-answering structure — a conditional that resolves itself — which makes it feel like distilled wisdom even though no one can say who distilled it. Greeting cards, posters and the 1972 Peter Max comic panel carried it to a mass audience under the honest label “Unknown.”

As it traveled, anonymous quotations tend to get “upgraded” with a famous author’s name for credibility. Gibran and Richard Bach — both associated with lyrical writing about love and freedom — were the natural landing spots, and the misattributions stuck.
context.pull: “The creator of this general saying is not known.”
